rationale: B wins because it is tighter and less padded: four real lanes, each with a harder editorial test attached. A has good material, but it lets weaker extrapolation in the door with “How a $26 billion private company keeps expanding without touching public markets,” while B’s “24,000 paid teams, 220 million users — and Canva can't name one enterprise customer” turns the missing proof into the story. A is useful; B is closer to what a real editor would greenlight after one phone call.
gaps_in_A: “Canva has converted just 24,000 of its 220 million users into paying teams” is sloppy math: users and paid teams are not the same unit, and “converted” is not in the fact block.
“IT departments were blocking it for” invents prior buyer behavior. The update gives SSO and admin tools, not evidence of blocked deals.
“growth funded by profit and an acquisition instead” overstates the finance angle. Profitable, private, and valued at $26B are supplied; capital strategy and funding source are not.
The fifth angle pads the set. “brand-safe image generation beats generic AI tools” may become a story, but the update only says on-brand generation and a recent unnamed acquisition.
gaps_in_B: “Canva can't name one enterprise customer” is sharper than the facts allow. The announcement did not disclose named customers; that is not the same as inability to name one.
“the exact moat Adobe has used to hold enterprise accounts” is plausible trade analysis, but not grounded in the supplied update. It needs proof or softer wording.
“then shipped it as a brand-safety feature” asserts causality between the acquisition and the launched AI feature, then admits the proof is missing. Good instinct, bad headline discipline.

The suggested next step, `newsjack-detector`, is a detour unless there is a specific external peg to hunt. The immediate job is proof: named customer, acquisition identity, enterprise-tier breakdown, and technical guardrails.
